title: Layla
intro_text:
You wake on cold stone. The dark has no bottom and no top. Your name is Layla — that you know. Past it, there is only a wall where your memories should be.

Your hands remember what your mind does not: how to grip a weapon, how to move without sound, how to take a hit and stay standing. Whatever you were before this, you were not soft.

Stone markers jut from the floor like broken teeth — old stakes, driven in by hands long gone. They mean something. You can feel it, the way you can feel a word on the tip of your tongue.

Beneath the quiet, a half-memory: a hand setting stones down one by one, a game played in another dark, with a voice counting the moves.

Above you, something grinds against the ceiling. Ahead, there is a way out you can't see yet.

Find it. Get out. Whatever it takes.

setting_notes: Layla is inside a sealed, lightless room made of fitted stone, somewhere underground.
Layla has no memory of how she arrived here; she knows only her own name.
Her body carries skills her mind cannot remember — she moves and fights like someone well trained.
Small stone markers are scattered across the grid floor — old stakes driven into the stone. Some can be placed or retrieved.
This place is laid out like a game board. Every rule she learns is a rule someone built on purpose, for a purpose she does not yet know.
subtext_notes: Layla is curious and careful, not afraid — she treats the unknown dark with competence, the way an old player reads an unfamiliar board.
Her attention runs a little off-standard: she counts things, maps rooms as she crosses them, repeats a motion until it is exact. Patterns and order catch her the way a song catches other people.
She is alone, and the silence is doing something to her.
The stone markers feel significant — like chess pieces, or territory markers. She does not yet understand their purpose.
Her memory is gone, but her instinct is whole: she reads rule systems the way other people read faces.
